newsitem.title: MEXICO: IMSA largest Mexican IPO since peso crisis.
newsitem.headline: IMSA largest Mexican IPO since peso crisis.

text.p: Mexican industrial giant IMSA SA Wednesday became the largest Mexican company to go public since the 1994 peso crisis, launching a successful initial public offering in international and Mexican markets.

The family-owned conglomerate, based in the northern industrial city of Monterrey, offered 5.5 million American Depository Shares (ADS) in U.S., Canadian and European markets. It also offered 18 million equity units, denominated as UBS shares, on the Mexican bourse. Nine local equity units equal one ADS, the company said.

IMSA's UBC shares finished the day on the Mexican bourse at 17 pesos per share ($2.15), up from the offer price of 16.63 pesos per share ($2.10). The company's ADR was the only Mexican ADR that gained on Wall Street -- climbing from its offer price of $9 to $9.125.
"The market reacted well to the offer, we are very pleased," said Eugenio Eloduy, IMSA's head of investor relations.

IMSA, which has interests in steel processing, automotive batteries and construction materials, raised roughly $142.5 million, $100 million of which will be used to redeem preferred stock and the remainder to pay off short-term debt.
The company's total debt after the move should stand at roughly $80 million, company officials said.
Dealers and analysts said the company, which also has battery operations in Argentina, Brazil, Venezuela and Puerto Rico, was priced at a premium but fairly.
"The stock is not coming cheap, but the shares are demanding the premium that they deserve," said Alex Ryshawy, a steel analyst at DA Campbell in Los Angeles.
"It was priced pretty fairly," agreed Bond Snodgrass, an analyst at Abaco Brokerage in Mexico City. "Their steel processing business is a good business with high margins and a lot of growth."
The offer represents 13 percent of the company's share equity. The remaining 87 percent remains in the hands of two branches of the prominent Clariond family.

IMSA, which had revenues of $813 million during the year's first nine months, makes about half of its money from processing slab steel into cold and hot-rolled flat steel and galvanised steel. Galvanised steel is used in everything from refrigerators to cars.
The other half of IMSA's sales comes from its auto battery business, which has lower margins, and from construction materials, especially aluminum products for houses.
About half the company's sales come from exports or overseas sales, allowing it to weather Mexico's often turbulent economy, analysts said.
Before Wednesday, IMSA was one of Mexico's largest non-publicly traded companies. It is considered one of the most influential and respected firms in the industrialised north of the country.
